assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 6,000 req/s peak. Mix: 55% nearby search, 28% business detail, 10% direct photo fetch, 4% review writes, 3% owner/business updates

assumptions.subject: geo
assumptions.statement: Cell-result cache hit-rate 75%, so only a quarter of searches reach the geo index. Every owner update re-indexes, which is why writes hit the index at 100%

assumptions.subject: geo
assumptions.statement: A geo-index instance sustains ~400 queries/s: a bounded quadtree/geohash cell lookup plus a distance sort over a few hundred candidates. This is the busiest component in the design

assumptions.subject: api
assumptions.statement: API tier ~1,200 rps/instance - heavier per request than a plain CRUD API because it merges search results, ratings and open/closed state

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Cache instance count (2) is HA plus working-set memory, not rps

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The SQL primary is modelled as ONE instance because there is one writer. A Multi-AZ standby is assumed in a real deployment but is NOT modelled as a second instance: it serves no traffic, and the engine would credit it with capacity it does not have. The engine will therefore flag the primary as a single point of failure - that flag is correct about failover, not about capacity.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: Business photos are served DIRECTLY from the object store in this reference - there is no CDN in the 7-component shape. That is why origin egress is ~250 TB/month. Putting a CDN in front is the first optimisation and would cut it by roughly 85%

assumptions.subject: pricing
assumptions.statement: Monthly usage volumes (egress/storage/requests) are derived from AVERAGE load = peak / 3; capacity and instance counts are sized to PEAK. A single system_rps cannot carry both, so the peak:average ratio is stated here rather than hidden in a volume.

assumptions.subject: pricing
assumptions.statement: Delivery egress is priced at the model's single flat internet-egress rate ($0.09/GB, the US first paid tier). At the petabyte-per-month volume this design implies, a real committed CDN contract is roughly 5-10x cheaper, so the egress line is an UPPER BOUND, not a quote. The volume (GB/month) is the engineering claim; the rate is not negotiated here.

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: Sharding the geo index by region, and ranking/personalisation of results, are OUT of this reference. A single logical index tier is modelled

_library.summary: Nearby-search over a geospatial cell index with cached results and a business-detail read path.
